strengths: The idea is rigorous and the implementation introduces a minimal overhead over an existing network.
The method is generic enough to be added to an arbitrary deep architecture
It performs well under varying experimental settings and architectures and can keep/improve upon its non-interpretable counterpart while greatly improving interpretability

The methodology and description of the model and inference process is soundly written. Modeling as the factorization matrices as Gamma distributions should, in theory, encourage sparsity. The variational inference process that is described makes sense.

Section 4 is an interesting addition to the paper, which describes how the factorization matrices are (partially) identifiable under certain assumptions, and how the author's model satisfies such criteria.
I appreciate the sanity testing for uncertainty/accuracy correlation in Section 5.1.1.
Suggested BDNL seems advantageous for uncertainty evaluation and disentangled representation learning.
The authors try to perform theoretical analysis of their method.
For most paragraphs ZeroGPT score was 0%, for some 4% and 8%. Thus rather human-written.
weaknesses: The distinction between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty is not clearly defined.
It is unclear how the proposed model ensures that epistemic uncertainty diminishes with increasing data.
The explanation of the uncertainty evaluation metric lacks clarity, particularly regarding the computation of n_ac, n_au, n_ic, and n_iu.
The difference between f_NN and f_lambda in Eq. 9 is not well-defined, making it difficult to understand their respective roles within the model.
The transition from Gaussian to Gamma distributions in section 3.2 is unclear and requires further justification.
The use of a fixed threshold of 10^-5 for sparsity measurement seems arbitrary; ideally, this threshold should be derived from an analysis of the weight distribution.
The significant performance difference observed when applying BNDL to ResNet versus ViT is not sufficiently explained.
The experiments are limited to a small set of interpretability baselines.
The framing of the Bayesian perspective in Sec 3.1 is rather crude; interpreting the input to a softmax as a delta distribution over a latent variable is not sufficient to be Bayesian.
The method lacks reparameterization and cannot be optimized (as noted in l218).
Equation (12) has an incorrect left-hand side; it should be p(Y|X) since you marginalize over θ and Φ on the right-hand side.
A short discussion or mention of last-layer Bayesian neural networks is missing.
The paper does not discuss related work on evidential deep learning (prior networks) that use similar mechanics.
The work lacks a reference to the seminal study on overconfidence by Guo et al. (2017) when discussing overconfidence in l167.
In Theorem 1, e_{(k)} is not introduced.
It is not clear why it is necessary to compare to non-Bayesian/point-estimate models, which obscures the core contribution of improved uncertainty quantification.
The reported PAvPU improvements for the ResNet model appear marginal and lack statistical significance analysis (e.g., confidence intervals or tests).
Sparsity values are not shown for competing approaches in Section 5.1.2.
The interpretability evaluation metric in Section 5.2 is questionable; the relevance of unsupervised disentanglement for ImageNet and CIFAR is not justified.
The paper does not compare to competing approaches in Section 5.2, lacking metric reporting and visualizations for those models.
The literature overview omits citations to works on DNNs and non-negative factor analysis within the interpretability framework.
Theorem 1 is not a proper theorem and its 'proof' is merely a discussion; the presentation should be revised.
The performance improvement does not seem significant; the paper lacks details on the number of repetitions, p-values, and calculation of the +/- numbers in Table 1.
